description: We are interested in someone who has done this before and can code.
summary: AnalogAtlas is an interactive research platform that identifies and characterises locations on Earth whose geological and environmental characteristics are comparable to regions on Mars and the Moon. It combines an interactive map with dated NASA satellite imagery, five Earth analogue sites, two planetary targets (Jezero Crater on Mars and the Marius Hills pit on the Moon), an explainable five-category similarity scoring system, and a fully traceable evidence trail — every number on the site links back to a public NASA, ESA, or other agency dataset or a peer-reviewed publication, and every limitation is stated openly.
details:
What the platform does

  1. Interactive map — a full-screen map (MapLibre GL) with a dark basemap and a dated NASA satellite imagery layer served directly from NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS). Users pick an imagery product (MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, or VIIRS) and an observation date; the map requests the corresponding image tiles from NASA on demand, with no API key and no paid service. Site markers open evidence panels for each location.
  2. Planetary targets — dedicated pages for Jezero Crater (Mars) and the Marius Hills pit (Moon), each presenting checked measurements, published references, and explicit statements of what is not yet known.
  3. Five Earth analogue sites — Salar de Uyuni (Bolivia), Mauna Loa (Hawaiʻi), Axel Heiberg Island (Canada), Makgadikgadi Pans (Botswana), and the Atacama Desert (Chile). Each site page presents terrain, climate, geology, and its specific analogy to the targets — including where the analogy breaks down.
  4. Explainable similarity scoring — a transparent, team-designed method (v1) with five weighted categories: geology (30%), landforms (30%), terrain (20%), temperature (10%), and water-related evidence (10%). Terrain and temperature are scored numerically from checked measurements (a logarithmic ratio where an exact match scores 100 and a tenfold difference scores 0). Geology, landforms, and water are scored with a visible three-criterion yes/no rubric based on published sources. Missing data is never scored as zero — it is excluded and reported as evidence coverage. Every score can be clicked through to the underlying evidence.
  5. Data & Methods and Limitations — a consolidated methodology section (datasets, processing steps, audit summary) and a standalone limitations page explaining where each analogy fails, what is modelled versus measured, and what the platform deliberately does not claim.

Verified measurements (processed by the team, reproducibly)

All numerical processing is done by documented, re-runnable Python scripts; the checked results ship with the site.

  • Jezero Crater terrain — NASA MOLA elevation data processed on a common ~463 m grid: 13,056 cells, of which 33.5% contain direct laser observations (the rest interpolated); mean resolved slope 2.76°. Elevations are never subtracted between planets because the reference surfaces differ.
  • Jezero ground temperature — Perseverance MEDA calibrated TIRS data (sols ~1050–1494, February 2024 – May 2025): ground temperature range 181.3–278.7 K (−91.9 to +5.6 °C), mean daily swing 70.8 K.
  • Earth terrain — Copernicus GLO-90 elevation audited on the same grid method for four sites; Atacama covered by a 49-point elevation sample (807–1,646 m, mean 1,098 m).
  • Earth climate — a complete 2024 ERA5 daily record for all five sites (366 days each, zero missing days), giving mean, extremes, daily temperature range, and precipitation.
  • Marius Hills pit (Moon) — LRO LOLA topography around the pit (median slope 1.00°, 12.8% of pixels steeper than 3°, 75.8 m local relief) and LRO Diviner bolometric temperatures (96.7–392.0 K). Pit dimensions (79–92 m funnel, 49–55 m inner width) are quoted from the LROC Pits Atlas, with a flagged disagreement in published depth estimates (10 m vs 40 m) that we report rather than resolve.

Honesty by design

The platform's central principle is that an analogue matches a process, not an entire planet. Accordingly:

  • Every figure carries an evidence label: checked (processed by us from a named dataset), reference (from a cited publication), connected (a live catalog request succeeded), or qualitative (team interpretation).
  • Nothing is invented: where no defensible data exists, the site says so and names the next research step instead of showing a number.
  • Scores are presented as a team method for explaining analogy strength — explicitly not mission certification and not a NASA standard.
  • Live dataset connections (NASA GIBS, Earthdata CMR, PDS Orbital Data Explorer) are discovery tools; a successful request is never presented as a validated measurement.

Technology

React 19 + TypeScript on TanStack Start; MapLibre GL with a keyless OpenFreeMap basemap; NASA GIBS WMTS imagery; Python processing scripts for MOLA, MEDA, GLO-90, ERA5, LOLA, and Diviner data; automated test suite (68 tests) covering scoring rules, data integrity, and navigation. No paid APIs, no user accounts, no stored credentials.

Current limitations (stated on the site)

  • Earth weather is modelled ERA5 air temperature at 2 m, while Mars values are measured ground temperature — only daily swing is compared, as a rough proxy.
  • The geological rubric is structured team interpretation of published sources, not automated mineral detection.
  • The Moon case study has checked terrain and temperature but lacks illumination, ice, regolith, and operations data.
  • Scoring weights are proposed team values; a sensitivity analysis under different weightings is planned future work
